newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: FEATURE - Kyrgyz orphanage forgotten in post-Soviet chaos.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kyrgyz orphanage forgotten in post-Soviet chaos.

text.p: Kuvat Aydrelleyev lay in a puddle of his own urine in a small room with blank white walls.
The six-year-old's thin, bare legs, paralysed after brain damage caused by lack of oxygen at birth, were marked with small, grey sores.

Kuvat was surrounded by 16 other children of widely differing ages and disabilities in the room at the Belovodskoye Home for Handicapped Children about 40 km (25 miles) east of Bishkek, capital of the former Soviet republic of Kyrgyzstan.
The children, with shaved heads, wore only rough white shirts.
There were no toys. Electricity had been cut. There was an overpowering smell of urine and faeces.

"We don't have any programme for them, they're not physically normal, they're idiots, we can't do anything for them," said Maxim Yelizanov, the home's director, wearing a winter coat and fur hat. "We don't give them toys as they'd just break them."
In adjacent rooms, handicapped children lay in bed, their thin, fragile bodies atrophied from lack of movement.
ABANDONED BY PARENTS
Most of the children, including Kuvat, had been abandoned by their parents. The staff themselves had difficulty remembering the names of the 160 children at the home.
Lars Gill, a Norwegian trained to work with handicapped children and now with the aid agency Save the Children in Kyrgyzstan, was visibly upset when he saw the skeletal body of four-year-old Aypiri.
"It's just a lack of care," he fumed. "If you stay in bed and you don't use your muscles, they just waste away. The only contact they have with adults is when they are fed."
Carers slopped spoons of soup into the childrens' mouths as they lay flat on their backs.
Gill had worked previously in the notorious orphanages in Romania. "The situation is worse than Romania when you take into account basic needs," he said.
Tatyana Rupyova, a harassed nurse in charge of dispensing medicines for the home, said: "We don't have enough medicines, clothes, we don't have any vitamins to give them."
Rupyova, who was working a 24-hour shift, earns $15 a month.
Gill aims to bring in toys and supplementary feeding for the children and training for the staff. But he admitted: "The toughest thing is to change attitudes."
OLD SOVIET SYSTEM STIGMATISED DISABILITY
Few in the remote, mountainous republic of 4.5 million know of the home's existence or of three others like it where conditions are said by Gill to be even worse.
An archipelago of institutions like Belovodskoye stretched across the former Soviet Union, where stigma was attached to disability, hidden away in small villages and forgotten.
The needs of such children are now drowned out by the storm of social and economic problems following Kyrgyzstan's independence five years ago.

"The children were isolated from society as they couldn't learn," said Tatyana Shamatova, the doctor on duty at Belovodskoye. "You can see how people look at these children. They just want to forget about them, the parents above all."
Nargiza Dzholdoshova, 11, was abandoned by her parents at birth. Her smiling eyes and sunny nature make her a favourite with the staff.
"I think there's nothing wrong with her, she could have gone to a normal school," said Shamatova.
But a yellowing document with an official stamp on Shamatova's desk decreed otherwise. Dzholdoshova's mental handicap was apparently forced on her by her surroundings.
EARLY DEATH FROM NEGLECT
The lack of adequate care condemns many to an early death. In 1995, 40 children died while 21 have died so far this year.
"A death rate of 25 to 30 percent is too high. We could avoid that," said Gill. "For many of these children, the home is a waiting room before death."

In Belovodskoye's Cemetery No.2, a row of bleached wooden crosses carrying no names mark the graves of the children who died at Belovodskoye. Unkempt marsh grasses threaten to make them disappear altogether.
"The parents don't even come to bury their children," said director Yelizanov. "They say they don't have enough money so we have to bury them ourselves."
